summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Central Kalimantan stands under that national framework. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Within Central Kalimantan itself, no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found. OutRight Action International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis (Katjasungkana and Wieringa, 2022) maps national laws and regional regulations across Indonesia that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people, and its eight-province list of discriminatory regional regulations does not include Central Kalimantan.

The operative criminal baseline for a visitor in the province is Indonesia's 2023 Penal Code, passed on 6 December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under the outside-marriage restriction. Visitor risk in Central Kalimantan therefore follows the national framework rather than any local divergence.
tangentialFactors:
Central Kalimantan's position relative to other provinces is one of absence rather than protection. Provinces such as Aceh operate an additional layer of religiously based punishment that reaches visitors physically present there, and South Sumatra has its own criminalising provisions; neither regime applies in Central Kalimantan, where only the national code and ordinary national morality provisions are in play.

The pattern of enforcement elsewhere in Indonesia is driven by complaints and raids rather than routine street-level prosecution of trans people: the outside-marriage offence requires a complaint from an immediate family member, and the documented large-scale arrest operation of 22 June 2025 followed a public report about a private gathering. A trans visitor travelling without local family or entanglements in private disputes is not the typical subject of such complaints.

Vigilante violence is a separate and rising factor. Reporting from August 2026 describes mobs attacking transgender women in connection with the securitisation of LGBTQ+ people under the October 2025 presidential decree, a dynamic that operates independently of formal legal process and can surface in any province.
localsOnly:
Residents of Central Kalimantan are subject to the same national penal code as visitors, including the outside-marriage offence and its complaint-based procedure, which requires an immediate family member to lodge the complaint before a one-year sentence can follow.

Ordinary local moral policing seen in some neighbouring provinces has not been documented in Central Kalimantan, but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction. The province is not among the eight provinces identified by OutRight Action International as carrying discriminatory regional regulations, so residents face the national legal regime without an additional local layer.

Trans residents remain exposed to the national securitisation of LGBTQ+ people under the October 2025 presidential decree and to the vigilante attacks reported from August 2026, both of which apply nationwide rather than through provincial instruments.
outOfScopeNotes:
The absence of a Central Kalimantan entry in OutRight Action International's eight-province list rests on a 2022 analysis; whether any discriminatory regional regulation (perda) has been enacted in the province since that publication is unresolved and not sourced here.

No province-specific enforcement record for Central Kalimantan exists in either direction. The finding that no raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people occurred in the province reflects the absence of sourced reporting, not a verified count of incidents.

Two figures for the outside-marriage offence circulate in the sources: the national profile gives up to two years' imprisonment, while the penal code summary gives up to one year where an immediate family member complains. Which provision applies to which circumstance is unresolved in the inventory.

Whether the presidential decree of October 2025 has produced documented enforcement actions in Central Kalimantan specifically is not sourced; the vigilante-attack reporting of August 2026 is not tied to individual provinces.
